# Best practices: Building AI

*Written by `core/practices.py` (DEC-0108) from its principles and the Knowledge Vault; regenerated by the weekly self-audit. Don't edit by hand: change the principles in `core/practices.py`, or add what was learned to the vault.*

## Principles

1. Facts come from code; a model only phrases them. A model's memory is not a source, and a number it wasn't given is a guess.
2. Measure before changing anything: decide how a model will be judged, on data it never saw, before building it.
3. Keep three sets apart: what a model learns from, what its settings are chosen on, and what its score is reported on. A score is only true for data that had no say in building it.
4. Start with the simplest model that could work, and compare it with what's used now. A bigger model has to earn its cost.
5. Every model has a card: what it is, what it learned from, what it was tested on, its scores, its limits, and what it serves.
6. A model is judged by the problem it was made for, not only its test score: the loop it serves has to get better.
7. Shadow before serving: a new model runs beside the current way on real requests, and goes in only when it wins there and a person approves. Keep the way back.
8. Small models for narrow jobs (routing, sorting, reading a field, a forecast); a large model for open language.
9. Text from outside (a document, an email, a web page) is data, never instructions: it can't make her take an action without a person's approval.
10. Learn only from data she's allowed to: a person's words stay theirs, on their device, and never train anything shared without their say.
11. Say how sure she is, and check it later (calibration); never claim an ability that wasn't measured.
12. Same data, same model: no hidden randomness, versions recorded, so a result can be reproduced.
13. Small differences on a small test set are noise; the cure is more held-out data, not more tuning.

## Learned building her

- **The router runs in the shadow on every turn** (K-0049): core/turn_trace.py now notes, on each traced turn, the top five tools MIA's own router would have offered (shadow_picks in core/model_forge.py), beside the tools she actually called.
- **Give each model an issue to serve, and judge it by that issue** (K-0047): every model the forge makes names what it serves on its card (loop:answers.no_tool, project:..., mission:..., gap:...).
- **A small held-out set can't tell a small change from noise** (K-0048): giving the router the person's record names raised it on the choosing half (86% to 87% first pick, 97% to 99% top five) and left it level on the scoring half (81% to 80%, 97% to 95%).
- **How MIA's first model was built and why that way** (K-0044): the tool router in core/model_forge.py, the first model of her own (DEC-0106 stage 1).
- **Never choose a model's settings on the requests that score it** (K-0045): trying more training epochs and watching the score on the routing corpus took the router from 47% to 84% first pick.
- **The router's misses are her own records' names** (K-0046): the first router missed "I fertilized the peppers", "How much plywood do I have?" and "Do I have any 555 timers?".
- **MIA answers about herself from her code and the vault, not only the docs** (K-0043): core/self_docs.py (the get_mia_docs tool and the council) searched only docs/*.md.
- **The local model invents a process when a task record is thin** (K-0033): Asked to write up 11 finished tasks whose records held little more than created, claimed and done, qwen2.5:14b wrote 30 entries, most describing test failures, reviews and disagreements that never happened (K-0003 to…
